10.1149/ma2026-01361763mtgabs.abstract: Green hydrogen powered by renewables has the potential to decarbonize the manufacturing of ammonia, methanol, and other critical chemicals, transforming the chemical industry. However, that opportunity will not be realized without green hydrogen attaining cost parity with the incumbent technology: steam reformed natural gas. In the case of proton exchange membrane (PEM) water electrolysis, cost reductions can be won via decreasing capital expenditures and through improvement of the electrical efficiency of the cell stack module. The anode porous transport layer (PTL) is a linchpin of this development strategy and the basis of this talk. We approached the problem systematically, investigating both the PTL itself and its interactions with the other cell components. Platinum is typically used as an antipassivation coating due to the small palette of materials capable of withstanding the high potentials of the PEM electrolyzer anode. Due to the high and volatile cost of Pt, we sought alternate materials systems for this coating via two routes. In the first case, thermochemical methods were used to harness the heat already used for PTL production in concert with an inexpensive reactant to induce the formation of titanium compounds on the surfaces of the PTL. In a parallel activity, we leveraged atomic layer deposition techniques to precisely deposit ultra-thin protective layers on PTLs. Concurrently, we used advanced forming techniques to optimize the structure of the PTL. This affects capital costs by improving the utilization of the precious iridium metal anode catalyst and lowers operational costs by protecting the thinner membranes required to attain low cell resistance (to wit, higher electrolysis efficiency). By engineering the pore size, porosity, and roughness of the PTL, we obtain high performance at ultra-low iridium loadings while simultaneously limiting anode damage and deformation. In combination, these advances provide a clear roadmap to next-generation porous transport layers. This talk will highlight key insights derived from these investigations.

10.1149/ma2026-01361766mtgabs.abstract: Porous transport layers (PTLs) are a critical component of proton exchange membrane water electrolyzers (PEMWEs) that must prove durable in harsh low-pH and high-voltage environments. Titanium sinters are the most cost-effective and promising PTL materials in these conditions, yet they passivate in the presence of oxygen, forming an insulative TiO 2 layer. As such, they require conductive anti-passivation coatings over the surface that are often deposited either by electroplating or by physical vapor deposition (PVD). PTL coatings are usually comprised of precious metals such as platinum, iridium, or gold. Platinum and iridium are reported to be the most stable over longer time periods due to the oxidation of gold above 1.5 V. 1 Even with conductive platinum and iridium coatings, uneven coverage can lead to pockets of TiO 2 growth, increasing the contact resistance of the PTL with the catalyst layer and causing voltage decay. 2 Because of this, most PVD or electroplated coatings are applied at thicknesses from 100 nm to 1 µm to ensure full surface coverage. 3 Even so, with a standard 100 nm PVD platinum-coated PTL, NREL estimates that PTL coating materials cost around $3 kW -1 at large PEMWE production quantities. 4 Atomic layer deposition (ALD) allows for the monolayer-by-monolayer growth of nanometer thick coatings on the surface of PTLs with conformal and continuous surface coverage at very low thicknesses. This has the potential to reduce the total amount of PGM metal needed to prevent titanium passivation. Additionally, ALD has a wide variety of precursors and methods that could be used to deposit platinum or non-precious metal coatings in parallel pathways toward making PTLs more economical for water electrolysis. In this work, we investigated the use of ALD to deposit 10 and 20 nm iridium coatings onto the surface of Mott titanium sinter PTLs and assess their feasibility for PEM water electrolysis compared to a thicker platinum coating benchmark. Not only do our ALD iridium coatings show a reduced interfacial contact resistance compared to platinum coatings due to their high conductivity in both the metallic and oxide state, but they allow for consistent PEMWE operation below 1.9 V for 1000 hours at 3 A cm -2 with no detectible voltage decay. This is an interesting result in itself, and serves as a stepping stone for exploration of the role ALD can play in the manufacture of porous transport electrodes to support further iridium reduction in PEMWE systems. 1 Liu et al. 10.1149/ma2026-01371840mtgabs.abstract: Electrocatalytic reduction of nitrate to ammonia offers a promising approach for remediation of nitrate-contaminated wastewater and the mitigation of carbon emissions as an alternative to the Haber-Bosch process. While considerable efforts have been made towards optimizing electrocatalysts, it is important to also consider how alkali metal cations (K+, Li+, Na+ and Cs+) may modulate NO3RR kinetics and the competing hydrogen evolution reaction (HER). Insights from similar reactions, such as CO2RR, suggest that cation identity can modulate cathode activity and faradaic efficiencies. Here, we study the effect of alkali metal cation identity and concentration on NO3RR kinetics, product selectivity, and the activity at silver (Ag) electrodes. Our results reveal stark differences in the magnitude to which cation identity impacts NO3RR by comparing acidic and alkaline environments. We consider these findings in light of the proton donor in these environments, where abstraction from water in alkaline environments may invoke unique roles for alkali cations. These findings demonstrate that tuning alkali metal cation identity can enhance NO3RR activity and highlights their critical role in modulating reaction kinetics.

10.1149/ma2026-01371915mtgabs.abstract: Ammonia functions as an effective energy carrier and alternative fuel, making it a critical component in the transition to resilient energy solutions. Additionally, it plays a vital role in modern agriculture, serving as a key component in nitrogen-based fertilizers that significantly boost crop yields to satisfy global food demands. Currently, however, ammonia production relies heavily on the energy- and carbon-intensive Haber-Bosch process, which requires large, centralized plants. This has led to an increased interest in on-site ammonia generation, which would reduce dependency on long supply chains, enhance energy security, and provide flexibility in energy use across various sectors, including agriculture, industry, and military applications. Electrochemical nitrogen reduction to ammonia offers a promising solution due to its distributed operation capabilities, high energy density, and ease of storage. This work focuses on lithium-mediated electrochemical ammonia synthesis (LiMEAS) in a non-aqueous medium as a promising method for decentralized ammonia production. By utilizing lithium’s effectiveness in breaking the strong nitrogen triple bond at ambient conditions to form lithium nitride (Li 3 N), which subsequently reacts with a proton source to generate ammonia, this research employs a high-throughput platform to facilitate rapid screening and provide a reliable statistical basis for analyzing key performance parameters. Recognizing the practical limitations inherent in practical distributed operations, we investigate the impact of air and water as direct inputs to the electrochemical reactor utilizing electrolytes commonly referenced in existing literature. Although the innovative cell design mitigates some of the negative effects associated with air and water inputs, it does not fully prevent performance degradation, particularly when water is introduced into the electrolyte. To address this performance decline, we examined various electrolyte additives and their effects on ammonia faradaic efficiency and yield in the presence of water. A key focus of this investigation was to understand the mechanistic role of the solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) in influencing the reaction pathway. This analysis yields essential insights into the robustness and viability of the system for on-site ammonia production in challenging operational environments, ultimately paving the way for more sustainable and resilient ammonia generation technologies. 10.1149/ma2026-01371916mtgabs.abstract: In industry, NH 3 is usually produced by the Haber-Bosch process, a synthesis technology that has been indispensable to human society for over a century. Still, the method operates at high temperatures (400-500°C) and high pressures (15-25 MPa). It consumes a large amount of hydrogen produced by fossil-fuel steam reforming to react with nitrogen, which requires more energy and has a high social cost due to its carbon footprint. In recent years, we have explored green ammonia production through photocatalytic and electrocatalytic N 2 reduction (PNRR vs. eNRR) and electrocatalytic NO 3 - reduction (eNO3RR). The 1% Ag-BiMn-based oxysulfide photocatalyst for PNRR achieved a high yield of ~3 mmol/g.h, but its yield remains much lower than the photo-H 2 yield. eNO3RR with a CuCo-based oxide/sulfide catalyst prepared by a hydrothermal route can yield above 44.6 mg/h.cm 2 with a single-stack cell. eNRR with a CuBi-based sulfur-oxide catalyst synthesized on a Ni foam by a chemical process can yield above 3.0 mg/h.cm 2 with an H-type cell. The yield rate follows the order: PNRR < eNRR < eNO3RR after laboratory self-calibration. PNRR and eNRR involve an inert, triple-bonded, non-polar N2 reactant, making their reactions challenging. The reaction micromechanisms are investigated.
10.1149/ma2026-01371916mtgabs.title: Development of the Ambient Green Ammonia by Three Routes

10.1149/ma2026-01371920mtgabs.abstract: Development of technologies for decentralised green ammonia (NH 3 ) production is one of the major challenges of this century, which will help to satisfy its progressively increasing demand in both fertiliser production and as a global carbon-free energy carrier, which is projected to reach ~690 Mt by 2050. ( 1 ) Among various approaches, electrochemical process based on the lithium-mediated nitrogen reduction reaction (Li-NRR) is the current most promising practical method that enables sustainable synthesis of NH 3 from renewables with very high faradaic efficiency and yield rate. Despite its short yet intensive development, the Li-NRR has achieved several key commercialisation benchmarks, including close to 100% faradaic efficiency, ( 2 ) practical yield rates, ( 2 ) and long-term stability. ( 3 ) One of the primary requirements for efficient performance of the Li-NRR is the continuous and sustainable transport of the protons from the anode to the cathode, a process that requires suitable carrier molecules. Besides that, it also influences the formation and properties of the solid electrolyte interphase (SEI). While ethanol proton carrier has been used in the initial as well as some of the latest important studies on the Li-NRR, including by us, its stability of under practical high-rate ammonia electrosynthesis conditions remains unverified. In some cases, alternative proton carriers like phosphonium cations ( 4, 5 ) and phenols ( 6 ) are used. Nevertheless, Li-NRR can still be operated without any dedicated proton carrier added though at a lower efficiency as compared to ethanol. It is hypothesised that here the decomposition and/or protonated products of solvent or the impurities within the electrolyte solution can transport protons. Alternatively, ammonia, the end product progressively accumulates in the electrolyte during Li-NRR which can contribute to protonation-deprotonation based transformations. Our current work explores this possibility, where the Li-NRR studies are performed with a high-performance lithium bis(trifluoromethylsulphonyl)imide (LiNTf 2 ) electrolyte in a robust two-compartment cell in the presence of NH 3 and/or NH 4 + . Our results demonstrate that the introduction of NH 3 to the electrolyte solution significantly improves the proton delivery to the cathode enabling high ammonia yield rate of 350 ± 40 nmol s –1 cm –2 and faradaic efficiency of 93 ± 6 % over 6 h experiments. Further the experiment has been operated for 48 h with only slight decreased performance. Conversely, introduction of NH 4 + degrades the Li-NRR performance likely due to its excessive proton donation capability, which promotes side reactions rather than Li-NRR. These results establish that the Li-NRR can be operated long-term without the state of art proton shuttle C 2 H 5 OH added. If this system can sustain in a more practical flow-cell setup it would simplify the NH 3 electrolyser technology and reduce overall system cost by eliminating an unnecessary and unstable compound. 10.1149/ma2026-01402042mtgabs.abstract: Artificial ammonia synthesis is vital to modern life; however, the Haber-Bosch process, by which most ammonia is synthesized, is capital- and carbon-intensive. Zero-valent-metal-mediated ammonia synthesis is a promising alternative but requires a metal that is both a strong reductant and forms a stable nitride. Only a small number of metals, like lithium, can satisfy these constraints. Therefore, we developed an electrochemical paradigm enabling the use of different reductants by orthogonalizing the roles of the zero-valent metal between sodium metal and a Ti active site. These components are cheaper than lithium by two orders of magnitude. Using a sodium-naphthalene-titanium cascade, we achieved a rate of 475 nmol cm -2 s -1 and a Faradaic efficiency of 24%, and found that the reaction rate depends primarily on current density.

10.1149/ma2026-01412090mtgabs.abstract: Controlling nanoscale morphology and phase composition during electrodeposition remains a fundamental challenge in the design of electrocatalysts and functional metal coatings. Here we introduce Complex Displacement Deposition (CDD), a new electrodeposition framework that couples metal-ligand coordination chemistry with a competitive precipitating agent (PA) to regulate when and how a solid phase nucleates during metal deposition. Unlike conventional methods that rely on uncontrolled local alkalinization, CDD decouples metal reduction from precipitation by using a PA that competes with the metal for the ligand only under specific interfacial conditions. This mechanistic separation enables precise control over precipitate formation, morphology evolution, and metal/oxide (or metal/complex) ratios. Using the Cu-citrate-Ca²⁺ system as a model, we identify and characterize a previously unreported mixed-metal complex, , which forms transiently at the electrode surface during deposition. Under reductive potentials, this phase repeatedly precipitates and is subsequently reduced, generating a self-templating precipitation–reduction cycle that yields highly porous metallic Cu deposit. The resulting high-surface-area copper exhibits exceptional activity for the nitrate reduction reaction (NO₃RR). In 0.5 M KOH + 100 mM NaNO₃, the optimized CDD-Cu catalyst achieves a partial current density toward NH₃ of 243 mA cm⁻² and a yield rate of 1.13 mmol h⁻¹ cm⁻² at -0.6 V vs RHE-values that surpass those of conventional electrodeposited Cu and commercial Cu/C catalysts. Despite modest Faradaic efficiency (≈64%), the magnitude of the NH₃ current on a pure metallic surface highlights the catalytic advantage conferred by CDD-enabled morphology control. Beyond the specific Cu-Ca-citrate case, CDD provides a chemically modular platform for tuning precipitation thresholds, ligand environments, and metal compositions. The approach is compatible with alloy systems and metals whose hydroxides/oxides are otherwise inaccessible electrochemically, opening new pathways for designing high-surface-area electrodes and metal–oxide composite films for electrocatalysis, sensing, and corrosion-resistant catalyst supports.

10.1149/ma2026-01422117mtgabs.abstract: The modern world is built on the creative application of the large scale industrialization of natural and synthetic processes. Some of these modern processes would be very familiar to humans from several thousand years ago such as large-scale agriculture or iron production. These sorts of processes are more efficient, mechanized, and perhaps performed on a larger scale, but are essentially unchanged from those used Millenia ago. However, other common processes such as aluminum or fixed nitrogen production would be entirely unrecognizable and are fundamentally different than they were performed even 150 years ago. Likewise, Idaho National Laboratory (INL) is investigating an industrial metabolism analog where concentrated nuclear thermal energy is substituted for diffuse solar radiation for the production of hydrocarbon resources. The INL thermosynthetic pathway directly mirrors photosynthesis and enzymatic carbon fixation with electrochemical cells, advanced catalysts, and thermal integration driving the looping conversion processes from thermal energy into complex chemical products. By tightly coupling the thermal and chemical processes along with recirculation of intermediate products the overall system provides a method to couple nuclear energy with existing hydrocarbon infrastructure. This approach represents a fundamentally new paradigm for industrial chemical and material production with similar intensification potential to that of the Haber-Bosch process.

10.1149/ma2026-01442799mtgabs.abstract: This poster introduces the research directions and laboratory capabilities of a newly established research group (PI: Fan Liu) at Penn State University, focusing on intermediate-temperature solid oxide electrochemical cells and heterogeneous catalysis for sustainable energy conversion and storage. The group aims to advance efficient and scalable electrocatalytic and thermal-catalytic systems through integrated efforts in materials synthesis, ceramic processing, interface engineering, device fabrication, and advanced characterization. Our research emphasizes the rational design of functional materials, including electrodes and electrolytes, oxide-supported metal catalysts, and liquid metal systems, to enable a range of energy-relevant reactions, such as hydrogen production, carbon dioxide conversion, ammonia synthesis/decomposition, dry reforming of methane, and natural gas upgrading. Particular attention is given to understanding structure-property-performance relationships across multiple length scales. A key strength of our program is the extensive use of both in situ and ex situ characterization techniques to probe reaction mechanisms and material evolution under realistic operating conditions. Leveraging the advanced facilities at the Materials Research Institute (MRI) at Penn State, we employ techniques such as in situ and operando FTIR-MS, TGA-MS, XRD, XPS, SEM TEM and Raman spectroscopy. These approaches enable direct observation of surface chemistry, phase transitions, and catalytic behavior under thermal and electrochemical stimuli. In parallel, our group actively collaborates with modeling teams to integrate experimental observations with theoretical insights, including density functional theory and data-driven approaches, to accelerate materials discovery and device optimization. This poster will provide an overview of our current capabilities, ongoing research efforts, and future directions, with the goal of fostering collaborations within the electrochemical and materials science communities.

10.1149/ma2026-01472324mtgabs.abstract: Electrocatalytic CO 2 reduction is an economically feasible approach for producing valuable chemical fuels and feedstocks. Cu is the only pure metal reported to be capable of producing high-value C 2+ products, such as ethylene, and has been studied extensively as a CO 2 reduction catalyst. 1 However, Cu undergoes electrochemical reconstruction through a dissolution-redeposition mechanism at relevant CO 2 reduction potentials. The electrochemical reconstruction of Cu has been shown to heavily influence the nature of active sites and, therefore, electrode activity, selectivity, and stability. 2 Most previous work has focused on investigating the identity of transient species that mediate reconstruction, as well as how catalyst properties such as nanoparticle size, shape, and oxidation state affect reconstruction. 2–4 However, there have been limited investigations on the role of the areal density of Cu nanoparticles on their surface reconstruction and how this influences reaction selectivity. In this work, we demonstrated plasma-enhanced atomic layer deposition (PE-ALD) 5 , as a useful tool for controlling the areal nucleation density of Cu-nanoparticles on a gas diffusion electrode (GDE), and investigated how this influences reaction selectivity. The influence of areal nanoparticle density on electrochemical reconstruction was investigated as a potential mechanism for the observed selectivity differences using in situ Raman techniques, as well as ex situ SEM and TEM imaging. Additional catalyst properties, such as quantified Cu loading via ICP-MS, were also investigated. These results highlight the importance of considering the areal density of nanostructures when evaluating selectivity in systems that undergo electrochemical reconstruction. 10.1149/ma2026-01472345mtgabs.abstract: Ammonia splitting has recently drawn significant research interest due to the reaction product, hydrogen, can be utilized as a clean, carbon-free chemical fuel.Electrocatalytic ammonia oxidation has been recently investigated since the kinetics of ammonia oxidation is sluggish due to multiple electrons and protons are involved, with a concomitant high overpotential. Various transition metal-based complexes have been synthesized as catalysts for ammonia oxidation. Ruthenium complexes, in particular, have shown promising performance and interesting reaction mechanisms. Several iron catalysts have also been reported, with fast kinetics but even greater overpotentials than ruthenium analogs. Instead of iron, we expect that moving down the periodic table to osmium will utilize higher energy d-electrons which will lower the redox potential of the molecular catalyst and enable lower overpotentials. In this presentation we will introduce the osmium analogs of two ruthenium complexes previously reported ([Os(tpy)(bpy)NH 3 ](PF 6 ) 2 and [Os(tpy)(dmabpy)NH 3 ](PF 6 ) 2 ) and investigations of the ammonia oxidation reaction chemistry. Both electrochemistry measurements and stoichiometric spectroscopic experiments are used to understand the reaction mechanism and unravel the rate limiting steps. There are some similarities to the mechanism reported for ruthenium complexes, but striking differences as well attributed to the greater backbonding ability of osmium compared to ruthenium. Switching from ruthenium to osmium has indeed lowered the overpotential since osmium complexes has a lower thermodynamic potential. Adding more electron-donating ligand, however, has shown a different behavior in this osmium analog by making the coordinated ammonia less acidic and therefore, slowing down the reaction. Considering the mechanism of the reaction, altering the pH of the solution, by using different supporting electrolytes, could also have an impact on the reaction mechanism and kinetics. The results of this study provide insights into the influence of structure (both ligand and metal center) on the catalytic activity and mechanism of molecular catalyst which will guide future designs of next generation ammonia oxidation catalysts as well as optimization of experimental conditions.

10.1149/ma2026-01472375mtgabs.abstract: The catalytic conversion of N 2 gas and NO 3 - ions into ammonia at ambient conditions through electrochemical and photoelectrochemical pathways offers an attractive alternative to the energy-intensive and high-carbon featuring Haber-Bosch process. Therefore, developing highly active, product-selective catalysts with good durability in a cost-effective manner is highly desirable. In this context, we studied vacancy-rich transition metal dichalcogenides for electrochemical NRR and NO 3 RR to produce ammonia. The sulfur vacancy-rich ex-MoS 2 demonstrated a high Faradaic efficiency of 69% with an ammonia yield rate of 5.56 mmol g cat –1 h –1 during electrolysis without a light source, which increased to 80% with a yield of 7.48 mmol g cat –1 h –1 under visible light illumination towards NO 3 RR. Similarly, selenium vacancy-rich ex-MoSe 2 achieved a Faradaic efficiency of 93.6% and a yield rate of 4.9 mmol gcat -1 h -1 during NO 3 RR. Additionally, ex-MoSe 2 showed an NH 3 yield rate of 933 μmol g cat –1 h –1 and an F.E. of 9.39%, while ex-WSe 2 reached 7.22% F.E. and a yield rate of 753 μmol g cat –1 h –1 towards NRR. DFT calculations support the binding of N 2 and NO 3 - species to the vacancies in these dichalcogenides, leading to the formation of *N, which is subsequently reduced to ammonia. 10.1149/ma2026-01502446mtgabs.abstract: This work shows the feasibility to use photoeletrosynthesis of ammonia and urea from dissolved N 2 and CO 2 in aqueous medium and seawater. Materials such as MFe 2 O 4 ferrite (M = Co 2+ , Cu 2+ and Mn 2+ ) and graphene were used as photocathode, operating as p -type and p-n homojunction semiconductors. The performance of CoFe 2 O 4 , CuFe 2 O 4, and MnFe 2 O 4 ferrites supported on GDL electrodes were tested in ammonia, fuels alcohols and urea formation by photoelectrocatalytic method. The main results highlighted the efficiency of all electrodes, but higher yield ammonia conversion, ethanol formation ant the best urea synthesis were obtained at GDL/MnFe 2 O 4 @FeOOH at -0.2 V vs Ag/AgCl/Cl - and artificial solar irradiation.

10.1149/ma2026-01502447mtgabs.abstract: Urea is conventionally synthesized through the Bosch–Meiser process, which involves reacting CO 2 with ammonia. Since ammonia is made using the Haber–Bosch process, the overall production of urea is quite energy-intensive. An electrochemical route for urea synthesis has been introduced as an energy-efficient alternative to meet the substantial demand. However, challenges of low Faraday efficiency and urea productivity have prompted numerous studies to overcome these obstacles. This talk addressed electrocatalytic urea synthesis using fluorine-doped strontium ferrite as a durable catalyst. It demonstrates superior performance in urea formation when fluorine doping regulated A-site vacancy for the structural reconstruction of catalytic surface under CO 2 atmosphere. The reconstructed fluorine-doped strontium ferrite catalyst achieved a high Faraday efficiency of 36 % and an impressive production rate of 2087 mgg - 1 h - 1 in an H-cell, with stability over 15 cycles. In-situ Raman spectroscopy identified reactive intermediates, and DFT results implied that the reconstruction of catalytic surface facilitates urea synthesis by providing more favorable electronic structure due to the lower d-band center of Fe for both C-N coupling and CO 2 reduction. These insights confirmed that a fluorine dopant can maintain the catalyst performance through its structural reconstruction as an endurable electrocatalyst.

10.1149/ma2026-01502448mtgabs.abstract: Metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) are porous coordination polymers of metal clusters coordinated by organic ligands to form one-, two- or three-dimensional structures. The fact that MOFs can be precisely engineered to obtain systems with adjustable pore sizes, controllable compositions with precisely formed (e.g., single atom) active sites permits, in principle, designing of electrocatalytic systems for specific reactions and applications. While the separated and monodispersed metal nodes (ions or clusters) of MOFs act as highly efficient active sites, the functionalized organic ligands could contribute to the chemical and structural selectivity with respect to both reactants and products. Various MOFs have been examined for electrochemical catalytic applications, such as energy conversion reactions, including hydrogen evolution, hydrogen oxidation, oxygen evolution and oxygen reduction reactions. Among transition metals, copper is of particular interest to electrocatalysis because the active sites of copper catalysts can be considered as alternative to those originating from noble metals. By analogy to noble metals, Cu has near-ideal binding affinity toward many molecular systems (e.g., O 2 , CO 2 , H 2 O, NO 3 - ) or reactive intermediates (e.g., CO, H 2 O 2 , NO x ). Copper-based MOFs) have been widely investigated for electrocatalysis, especially for the electrochemical reduction of carbon dioxide. In principle, the Cu-based MOFs could help to stabilize both Cu + and Cu 2+ species, optimize the charge transfer at the electrocatalytic interface, and to improve the activity and selectivity. Copper coordination compounds are well-known to react with dioxygen , and their performance has been found by us closely associated with the metal/ligand combination therein. It has also been postulated that Cu exhibits an optimum adsorption energy for activation of nitrates and an adequate selectivity toward ammonia as final product. In the present study, we consider a novel MOF composed of repeated spatial or planar patterns of copper ions coordinated to organic ligands through covalent bonds. The structural motif describing the coordination environment of copper centers is comparable to the framework of HKUST-1 built up of dimeric copper units connected by benzene-1,3,5-tricarboxylate linker molecules. When it comes to electrocatalytic applications, among important issues are the presence of copper sites, their coordination geometry and accessibility of redox transitions involving Cu II , Cu I or even Cu 0 species. It is reasonable to expect that the existence of various redox forms of copper, in addition to the layered MOF structure, should facilitate electron transfers and improves catalytic currents. Two new Cu-based MOF structures (abbreviated as TUW-1 and TUW-2) have been considered as catalytic materials in the present study. These structures have been made from Cu 2+ ions in combination with mixed organic linkers marked by nitrogen donor and carboxylate coordination sites, and they demonstrate long-term stability in various aqueous solutions. The TUW-1 and TUW-2 MOFs exhibit certain structural differences: while TUW-1 features bidentate bridging coordination of carboxylates to Cu II centers and hydrogen-bonded bpe (i.e., trans-1,2-bis(4-pyridyl)ethene) molecules, In comparison to HKUST-1, where all three btc carboxylates coordinate to Cu II and no free acidic groups remain, Differences in sterics and electronics of the primary coordination sphere should lead to distinct binding of O 2- and H 2 O molecules, or nitrate molecular anions, thus influencing their catalytic electroreductions. TUW-1 and TUW-2 provide additional adsorption sites and enhanced framework durability. The results reported herein are consistent with the appreciable electrocatalytic activity of TUW-1 and, particularly, TUW-2 toward reduction of oxygen, conversion of nitrates to ammonia, in addition to hydrogen evolution. Introduction More than half of the world’s population is dependent on synthetic nitrogen-based fertilizers which are produced via the Haber-Bosch process. Besides approximately 1% of the world’s annual energy supply going into this process [1], it is carbon intensive in the form of requiring methane and is responsible for approximately 1% of global anthropogenic CO 2 emissions [2]. This along with the logistics of ammonia transport make more localized processes, that can reuse other agricultural wastes, a topic of recent interest. For raw waste, ammonia or other nitrogen compounds can make up a large portion of the ionic content along with phosphorus, potassium, and calcium containing species [3]. However, during certain processes other compounds might be added in high amounts such as the process of Botte et al. (2024) using 0.1 M NaOH [4]. As such, analytical techniques are necessary for monitoring the inflows and outflows of such processes and CE is frequently named as a “green” alternative to other analytical techniques such as liquid chromatography [5]. 10.1149/ma2026-01562708mtgabs.abstract: We propose a unified electrochemical separation platform for the selective recovery of resources from complex aqueous waste streams, including nitrogen, mineral salts, and organic species. The overarching goal is to convert high-salinity and nutrient-rich wastewaters into value-added products through electrochemically driven, adsorption-based separations. This approach reduces energy consumption, chemical use, and waste generation while advancing a circular economy for water, materials, and nutrients. An integrated electrochemical–adsorption reactor has been developed for nitrogen removal and recovery that couples nitrogen conversion with biogas upgrading. In contrast to conventional activated sludge treatment and Haber–Bosch-based nitrogen management, this system enables the direct transformation of aqueous nitrogen species into solid nitrogen-containing fertilizers under ambient conditions, without the need for external chemical oxidants or reductants. An applied electrochemical driving force controls nitrogen speciation and transport, while selective adsorbent media capture and concentrate ammonium and other nitrogen species into recoverable solid products. Concurrently, the reactor facilitates biogas purification, producing upgraded renewable natural gas. This approach promotes circular nitrogen management by closing the loop between wastewater treatment and fertilizer production, minimizing nutrient discharge and reducing reliance on primary nitrogen fixation. In addition, selective extraction of mineral salts using Electrochemical Adsorbent Separation Technology (EAST) will be discussed. Collectively, these efforts demonstrate the versatility of electrochemical adsorbent separation as a platform for the selective and resource-efficient recovery of both critical materials and nitrogen-based products from challenging aqueous streams. By integrating ion-selective adsorption with electrochemical driving forces in modular architectures, this technology enables process intensification, supports water reuse and resource recovery, and provides a scalable pathway toward a circular economy for energy, materials, and nutrients.

10.1149/ma2026-018744mtgabs.abstract: We use transition metal chalcogenides to facilitate the nitrate reduction to ammonia (NH 3 ) and proton reduction to hydrogen (H 2 ) via dark and photo electrocatalysis. The electrochemical nitrate reduction reaction (NO 3 RR) presents a promising route to generate NH 3 from nitrate for fuel and fertilizer applications. This study investigates a polycrystalline vanadium sulfide (VS X ) electrocatalyst, derived from annealed solvothermally grown VS 2 , which exhibits exceptional activity (2.3 ± 0.6 mg·cm–2·h–1 @ –0.92 V vs RHE) and Faradaic efficiency (69 ± 6% @ –0.69 V vs RHE) for NO 3 RR in a neutral pH electrolyte. Grand-canonical density functional theory (GC-DFT) simulations identify sulfur vacancies in VS 2 as key active sites for NO 3 – adsorption and NH 4 + production, where NO 3 – outcompetes H + for adsorption. The GC-DFT shows multiple favorable reaction mechanisms at undercoordinated V sites. This work highlights the role of material engineering in enhancing NO 3 RR activity and provides insights into the mechanism and active site characterization for ammonia synthesis using vanadium sulfides. In addition to NH 3 generation, we are interested in photoelectrochemical H 2 generation using MoS 2 monolayers interfaced with GaInP. We show that MoS 2 monolayers on GaInP have exceptional performance for > 100 h of H 2 generation and this outperforms bare GaInP. We provide mechanistic detail for the durable performance and protection of the GaInP semiconductor.

10.1201/9781003782254-151.abstract: Hydrogen (H 2 ) stands as the leading alternative to fossil fuels due to its renewable nature, exceptional energy-carrying capacity, and zero carbon dioxide emissions. Researchers increasingly favor large-scale H 2 production via water electrolysis powered by renewable energy, with water splitting being a viable method for long-term, sustainable energy storage. Noble metals efficiently catalyze the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER), but the performance of water electrolysis largely depends on the activity of the electrocatalysts. To further advance renewable energy technology, researchers are developing highly efficient, stable, cost-effective, and less toxic catalysts like CuO, NiO, Co 3 O 4 , FeP/FeP 2 , CoP/Co 2 P, MoP, and NiCo 2 O 4 . Single-atom catalysts (SACs) have gained significant attention for their exceptional catalytic activity and high atom-utilization efficiency. Atomic Layer Deposition (ALD) has become one of the most effective methods for fabricating SACs due to its precise ability to deposit small atoms uniformly. This paper explores the recent advancements in SAC synthesis for HER, focusing on the ALD technique to enhance catalytic efficiency and performance.

10.20944/preprints202607.0631.v2.abstract: The Zeta-Minimizer Theorem (ZMT) furnishes a rigorous axiomatic foundation for thermodynamics through three principles—strict concave entropy maximization, uniform Gibbs free energy landscapes with spectral minima, and irreducibility enforced by perpetual bounded oscillations—augmented by helical geometry in which prime numbers emerge as indivisible cycle lengths. The multi-component grand-partition function Z(s) is constructed and establish its universal categorical invariance under functorial mappings, thereby providing a parameter-free backbone for equilibrium and dynamical phenomena. From this structure the thermodynamic conjugate pairs and variational Maxwell relations, the emergence of chemical equilibrium and the equilibrium constant are deductively derived directly from the grand potential, explicit fugacity coefficients, and a variational reaction-rate law governed by the analytical scalar Hessian of the gas-phase reaction coordinate. For heterogeneous systems solid–fluid interface continuity conditions, marginal stability criteria via the covariant fugacity Hessian are obtained, and—crucially—the first-principles deductive origin of linear scaling relations and Sabatier volcano plots from closed prime functions, without empirical parameters. A complete methodology is developed for ammonia-synthesis loop analysis and catalyst optimization. Central to this methodology is the vapor–solid (V/S) locus, which incorporates inert effects, promoter-induced shifts in effective black-box constants, and distinct operating regimes of Fe- versus Ru-based catalysts. Numerical integrations and Hessian-based kinetic analyses quantitatively recover industrial third-bed behavior, elucidate the lab–industry gap in recent low-pressure studies, and furnish predictive guidelines for next-generation catalyst and process design. The ZMT framework thereby bridges number-theoretic structure with practical chemical engineering, offering zero-adjustable-parameter predictions for sustainable ammonia production.
10.20944/preprints202607.0631.v2.title: The Zeta-Minimizer Theorem: A Deductive Axiomatic Framework for Variational Thermodynamics, Chemical Equilibrium, and Heterogeneous Catalysis with Applications to Ammonia Synthesis

10.21203/rs.3.rs-10361076/v1.abstract: Abstract The aim of this study carried out is to enhance the sensing performance of the pure material through a doping strategy. Ammonia is one of the toxic gases present in the atmosphere, released mostly from industries and agricultural pesticides, which leads to serious health issues when inhaled. A semiconducting metal oxide sensor based on a chemi-resistive mechanism is a well-known candidate in the field of sensing and detecting vapours. BaSnO 3 , an established oxide perovskite material because of its versatility and flexible properties. Undoped and nickel-doped BaSnO 3 (BaSn 1-x Ni x O 3 , x = 0.1, 0.3M) samples were prepared via solid-state reaction. The synthesized powder sample was then coated onto a glass substrate through the spin-coating technique. The XRD pattern confirms the cubic perovskite structure. FESEM micrographs reveal the porous nature and smaller particle size with moderate agglomeration. BET analysis found a high surface area and appreciable pore diameter. The gas sensing performance towards ammonia was successfully evaluated. With a lower limit of detection, the sample exhibited a high response voltage at an operating temperature of 300 °C. Additionally, it also provides enhanced sensitivity, good selectivity, excellent repeatability and high stability over a period of time, which are major parameters required for a gas sensor. Comparatively, BaSnO 3 doped with a low molar concentration of nickel has exhibited superior performance over other samples. So, it is highly recommended for Chemi-resistive gas sensing application in detection of ammonia.

10.21203/rs.3.rs-9940166/v1.abstract: Catalytic dinitrogen (N 2 ) fixation commonly proceeds through metal nitride intermediates, yet their subsequent hydrogenation is often thermodynamically challenging, because the first hydrogenation step converts a stable metal nitride into a high-energy parent metal imide, where formation of a weak N-H bond provides little thermodynamic compensation. Here we report a distinct photochemical pathway for molybdenum nitride activation that enables direct nitride-to-amide conversion by hydride transfer for ammonia synthesis. Mechanistic studies show that visible-light excitation of 4DPAIPN generates an isolable dihydroacridine derivative, PAC-AcrH 2 , whose structure was established by single-crystal X-ray diffraction. Isolated PAC-AcrH 2 functions as a photohydride donor when pre-associated with protonated molybdenum nitride complex. Visible-light excitation promotes nitride hydrogenation through a stepwise electron-proton-electron sequence on the femtosecond-to-nanosecond timescale. This reactivity is distinct from conventional photoinduced proton-coupled electron transfer pathways and provides a kinetically efficient route toward nitride-to-amide conversion. These findings identify an unexplored mode of metal nitride activation and provide a framework for designing light-driven N 2 reduction systems based on excited state hydride transfer.
10.21203/rs.3.rs-9940166/v1.title: Ultrafast Hydride Transfer Pathway in Dinitrogen Fixation

10.2139/ssrn.7036029.abstract: Earth-abundant materials combined with scalable fabrication methods are essential for advancing photoelectrocatalytic technologies for sustainable fuel production and water purification. In this study, we report a novel process for fabricating SnxFe2-xO3 photoelectrodes using atomic layer deposition (ALD), which provides angstrom-level thickness control, excellent scalability and conformal coating of complex 3D substrates, making it a promising technique for advanced thin film photoelectrode fabrication. Tin doping was achieved through a supercycle ALD approach. A Box-Behnken Design (BBD) based response surface methodology was employed to systematically optimize the synthesis parameters. The total number of ALD cycles, fraction of SnO2 cycles, and post-deposition annealing temperature were selected as independent variables, while photocurrent density at 1.6 V vs RHE and photocurrent onset potential in a neutral phosphate buffer electrolyte were used as response parameters. Structural, compositional and morphological properties were characterized using multiple techniques. The statistical model revealed strong correlations between synthesis parameters and photoelectrocatalytic (PEC) performance, enabling identification of optimal synthesis conditions. The optimized SnxFe2-xO3 photoelectrode exhibited enhanced PEC activity for antibiotic degradation, and the underlying degradation mechanism was elucidated.
10.2139/ssrn.7036029.title: Atomic layer deposited SnxFe2-xO3 photoelectrodes: Box-Behnken design guided optimization for enhanced photoelectrocatalytic performance and antibiotic degradation

10.2139/ssrn.7070298.abstract: In order to carry out electrochemical nitrate reduction efficiently, the catalytic electrodes should be able to initiate the reaction at the surface of the electrode and further catalyze the transformation of the intermediates of nitrate to ammonia. In this work, Fe was added to a CuCo electrodeposited frame to fabricate CuCoFe/Ni foam cathodes for nitrate-to-ammonia conversion to further enhance intermediate hydrogenation and catalyst mass utilization. The CuCoFe electrode obtained by direct current (DC) electrodeposition removed 96.0% of NO3-N in 1 h and the maximum NO2-N accumulation was 4.5% with a faradaic efficiency of NH3 of 91.0%. The catalyst architecture was also controlled by pulse-reverse potential electrodeposition which reduced the amount of deposited catalyst and enhanced the electrochemically active surface area and interfacial charge transfer. The optimized pulse-reverse CuCoFe catalyst achieved the highest NO3-N removal of 96.82%, the lowest NO2-N peak of 3.75% and the lowest NH3 production mass normalized of 0.408 mmol h-1 mg-1, which is about 1.9 times that of the directly deposited CuCoFe electrode. Based on structural and electrochemical characterization, along with studies of the reduction of nitrite, it is suggested that the improved performance is due to the combined activities of Cu, Co and Fe. Cu promotes the activation of NO3 and the formation of NO2, while Co/Fe sites promote further hydrogenation of NO2, leading to greater consumption of the intermediate and increased selectivity towards ammonia. This design using Fe as a catalyst offers a potential mass efficient and intermediate-conversion approach to nitrate remediation and ammonia recovery with non-noble-metal electrodes.
10.2139/ssrn.7070298.title: Pulse electrodeposited Cu-Co-Fe trimetallic catalysts for highly efficient and selective electrochemical nitrate reduction to ammonia

10.2139/ssrn.7081550.abstract: The electrocatalytic reduction of nitrate to ammonia over copper-based catalysts in neutral electrolyte presents an environmentally benign alternative to the conventional Haber–Bosch process. However, the practical application of Cu-based catalysts is severely constrained by an insufficient supply of active hydrogen (*H) at Cu sites, which limits both the ammonia yield rate and Faradaic efficiency. Herein, a delafossite-type CuCoO2 electrocatalyst was successfully constructed through a B-site metal regulation strategy and applied to electrocatalytic nitrate reduction to ammonia under neutral conditions. It found that the optimized CuCoO2 catalyst achieves a remarkable ammonia Faradaic efficiency of 98% and an ammonia production rate of 18.04 mg h-1 cm-2, substantially surpassing the performance of reference Cu2O (FE: 62%; yield rate: 10.08 mg h-1 cm-2). Mechanistic investigations, combining Bode plot analysis and in situ Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy, reveal that the inferior performance of Cu2O originates from its limited *H supply, which leads to the excessive accumulation of nitrite (NO2-) intermediates on the catalyst surface. In stark contrast, the superior catalytic performance of CuCoO2 is attributed to the synergistic interplay between Cu and Co dual-atom active sites co-located within the same delafossite lattice. This atomic-scale synergy markedly enhances the generation and utilization of active hydrogen, enabling the efficient consumption of nitrite species accumulated on Cu sites and thus driving the complete eight-electron reduction of nitrate to ammonia with high selectivity. These findings establish a new structural paradigm for the rational design of next-generation electrocatalysts for nitrate reduction to ammonia, and provide critical theoretical insights into the role of atomic-scale bimetallic synergy in overcoming the intrinsic limitations of single-metal catalysts.
10.2139/ssrn.7081550.title: Delafossite-type CuCoO2 for efficient electrocatalytic nitrate reduction to ammonia in neutral electrolyte

10.2139/ssrn.7100193.abstract: The lithium-mediated nitrogen reduction reaction (Li-NRR) is a promising electrochemical pathway for ambient NH3 synthesis, yet its efficiency remains limited by dendritic Li plating, parasitic reactions, and interfacial instability. Here, we introduce electrospun artificial solid electrolyte interphases (SEIs) on gas diffusion electrodes (GDEs) as an effective strategy to improve the performance of Li-NRR flow cells. In this system, an effective artificial SEI should simultaneously stabilize the electrode–electrolyte–gas triphase interface and guide the formation of a favorable interphase for uniform Li plating. Among the examined polymers, poly(vinylidene fluoride-co-hexafluoropropylene) (PVDF-HFP) was the most effective, providing a fibrous scaffold that reacts with Li during operation and induces a LiF-rich SEI. Morphological and spectroscopic analyses indicate that a LiF-rich interphase forms preferentially along the polymer fibers, consistent with more uniform Li plating and controlled SEI growth. As a result, the optimized electrode achieves a Faradaic efficiency (FE) of 65.5 ± 7.4%, compared with 43.2 ± 2.7% for bare stainless steel (SS) mesh under identical conditions. In addition, the gaseous fraction of produced NH3 increases by more than threefold, consistent with improved preservation of the triphase interface and gas-transport pathways. This work highlights electrospun artificial SEIs as a promising design strategy for Li-NRR flow cells.

10.2139/ssrn.7117864.abstract: In view of the fact that the existing absorbing materials are difficult to take into account the comprehensive indexes of thin, light, wide and strong, the technical bottlenecks of high energy consumption and long cycle of traditional preparation process, this study combines polymer-derived ceramics (PDCs) and Joule rapid heating process to prepare high-performance SiCN aerogel. Raman characterization results confirm that the Joule heating sample has higher defect density and smaller graphite domain size, and can introduce more polarization loss sites than the tube furnace sample. Prepared via rapid sintering at 1100 °C, the PDN-1100 sample exhibits an RLmin of -53.49 dB at an ultrathin thickness of 1.55 mm and an EAB of 5.25 GHz, featuring strong attenuation and a broad absorption band. Microscopic and phase analysis show that the wave absorption performance of the material is synergistically regulated by the degree of graphitization and multiphase interface, and multiple losses work together to efficiently dissipate electromagnetic waves. The radar cross section simulation proves that the far-field stealth control ability of the material is outstanding. After the superstructure optimization, the radar cross section suppression effect is 14.61 dBm2 higher than that of the ideal conductor, which has excellent stealth application value. Relying on this material to build a stealth antenna model, it can provide support for the engineering landing of equipment stealth. This study reveals the internal mechanism of Joule heating regulating the microstructure and dielectric loss of SiCN aerogels, and offers a novel strategy for designing lightweight, high-performance electromagnetic stealth materials.
10.2139/ssrn.7117864.title: Fabrication of SiCN Aerogels by Joule Heating: Highly Efficient Preparation of Ultrathin Broadband Absorbing Materials for Radar Stealth Applications

10.2139/ssrn.7118380.abstract: The stable mullite structure in fly ash (FA) and the stubborn olivine structure in spent lithium iron phosphate cathode materials (SLFP) are the core challenges restricting the metal resource utilization of these two types of solid wastes. This study innovatively proposes a new method of flash Joule heating (FJH) synergistic conversion of SLFP and FA (SLFP-FJH). This strategy utilizes the high-temperature shock generated during the FJH process to induce an in-situ reaction between SLFP and FA. Among them, the Li+ and Fe2+ released by the decomposition of SLFP act as charge compensation ions, effectively balancing the negative charge gap produced by [AlO4]5- replacing [SiO4]4- in mullite, promoting the fracture of the stable Bridging Oxygen in mullite and reconstituting the highly active amorphous glass phase. The effects of material ratio, FJH treatment temperature and time, and leaching agent concentration on metal leaching were systematically investigated. Combined with XRD, FT-IR, Raman and XPS, the structural evolution mechanism and charge balance mechanism of mullite transformation to amorphous phase were revealed. Kinetic studies indicated that the leaching process of the SLFP-FJH product conformed to the Avrami model. The results show that after treatment at 1800 °C for 8 s, 99.84% of Al and 99.77% of Li can be leached, and the leaching rate of Fe reaches 77.22%. Compared with traditional pyrometallurgical or hydrometallurgical processes, this technology demonstrates significant advantages in terms of processing cost and process simplicity, providing a brand-new strategy for achieving high-value utilization of solid waste and closed-loop recovery of lithium iron resources.
10.2139/ssrn.7118380.title: Spent Lithium Iron Phosphate-Mediated Flash Joule Heating for Inducing Amorphization Transformation of Fly Ash towards High-Efficiency Recovery of Valuable Components

10.2139/ssrn.7168940.abstract: The rapid expansion of electric vehicles and artificial intelligence–driven technologies has accelerated the demand for lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) with enhanced lifespans and safety. Atomic layer deposition (ALD) has emerged as a promising surface engineering technique for stabilizing high-nickel cathodes. However, systematic comparisons between powder and electrode ALD strategies remain limited. In this study, ZrO₂ coatings fabricated via powder and electrode ALD processes were systematically compared using LiNi0.8Co0.1Mn0.1O2 (NMC811) cathodes. Among the investigated conditions, the powder ALD strategy exhibited the best electrochemical performance, delivering a discharge capacity of 172.49 mAh g⁻¹ with an outstanding capacity retention of 95.8% after 200 cycles. Microstructural analysis revealed that powder ALD formed a highly conformal and uniformly distributed ZrO₂ stabilization layer directly on individual active particles, whereas electrode ALD resulted in relatively non-uniform coating distribution within the porous electrode structure. Impedance and post-cycling microstructural analyses further confirmed that powder ALD effectively suppressed impedance growth, particle cracking, and surface structural degradation during prolonged cycling. These findings demonstrate the strong potential of powder ALD as a practical and scalable interface engineering strategy for long-lifetime, high-energy-density LIBs.
10.2139/ssrn.7168940.title: Interfacial Stabilization of High-Nickel NMC Cathodes: A Comprehensive Approach using Powder and Electrode Atomic Layer Deposition Methods

10.2139/ssrn.7181494.abstract: Complex oily wastewater contains emulsified oil and dissolved organic contaminants, yet conventional membranes mainly separate phases and provide limited removal of soluble pollutants. Here, we report an NCF/PTF catalytic separation membrane that integrates a nitrogen-doped carbon felt electrothermal catalytic layer (NCF) with a superhydrophilic/underwater superoleophobic polyacrylonitrile (PAN)-based separation layer formed by surface segregation. The membrane was evaluated for surface chemistry, wettability, electrothermal response, oil-water separation, dye degradation, and the catalytic mechanism. The NCF/PTF can reject oil and achieve high oil rejection (＞98%) for oil-water mixtures and emulsions (＞96%), whereas the conductive NCF layer generates localized Joule heat under a low-voltage field to activate PMS and degrade dissolved dyes, achieving the dye removal ratio exceeding 99%. Furthermore, the NCF/PTF can maintain high-efficiency oil rejection and dye removal ratios for complex wastewater containing oil and dye, even after five consecutive cycles, solely through filtration, demonstrating its ability to enable in situ, one-step purification of complex oily wastewater. This work provides a design route for coupling interfacial separation with localized advanced oxidation, representing the future direction of complex wastewater treatment.
10.2139/ssrn.7181494.title: A Joule-Heating-Driven Superwetting Membrane for One-Step Complex Wastewater Purification

10.2139/ssrn.7211156.abstract: Electrocatalytic nitrate reduction to ammonia (NO3RR) is a promising approach for simultaneous nitrate removal and sustainable ammonia synthesis under ambient conditions. Herein, a copper foam-supported cobalt-tannic acid-modified copper nanowire electrode (Co-TA/Cu NW) was constructed for efficient NO3RR. The conductive Cu nanowire array provides abundant active sites and rapid electron transport, while the Co-TA interfacial layer regulates the local electric field to promote nitrate enrichment and suppress the competing hydrogen evolution reaction. As a result, the Co-TA/Cu NW electrode achieves a high NH3 Faradaic efficiency of 98.71% and an NH3 yield rate of 5.99 mg h-1 cm-2 at -0.63 V vs. RHE in 0.2 M K2SO4 + 0.01 M KNO3. The electrode also exhibits low nitrite selectivity, good stability, and excellent performance under dilute nitrate conditions. This work provides an effective strategy for interfacial regulation toward enhanced nitrate-to-ammonia electrosynthesis.
10.2139/ssrn.7211156.title: Construction of a Copper Foam-Supported Cobalt-Tannic Acid-Modified Copper Nanowire Composite Electrode for Interfacial Electric Field-Enhanced Nitrate Electroreduction to Ammonia

10.2298/tsci260121096y.abstract: In this study, A three-dimensional multiphysics model coupling electric and thermal fields was developed to systematically explore the effects of microscopic structural parameters (wire diameter and spacing) on current density distribution, Joule heat source characteristics, and temperature field uniformity within the Joule heating catalyst support (JHCS).The results indicated that increasing the wire diameter directed current shunt toward the branch channels, thereby improving heat generation uniformity. Conversely, increasing the wire spacing led to current "dead zones" in the branch channels due to increased electrical resistance. This non-uniformity was further amplified because Joule heat was proportional to the square of the current density. The temperature field was primarily governed by the heat transfer radius determined by the pore size of the JHCS; excessively small wire diameters or large spacings resulted in significant low-temperature zones at the channel centers. Synthetically, a wire diameter of 0.10 mm and a wire spacing of 0.25 mm were identified as the optimal structure, achieving a balance between heat generation efficiency and thermal uniformity.

10.24425/cpe.2026.158127.abstract: In light of the current efforts of harnessing hydrogen as a potential carbon free energy source alternative to fossil fuels, ammonia has emerged as one of the possible candidates for an effective hydrogen storage method, due to its significantly simplified storage conditions. In this work, the Haber-Bosch process for ammonia synthesis was studied for three scales of production, in the aspect of energy efficient reactor design and optimal operational conditions, with the use of a process simulator, allowing for the manipulation of desired plant parameters in a wide range of values. Moreover, the energy balance of the process has been included in the research process allowing for the visualization of energetic cost of increasing the energy density of the system. The obtained data provides a basis for analysing the Haber-Bosch process in the context of ammonia conversion for hydrogen storage.

10.25092/baunfbed.1888785.abstract: In the presented study, green synthesis of Cu nanoparticles was achieved in Camellia sinensis (green tea) plant extract. The polyphenolic natural components abundant in Camellia sinensis extract reduced Cu2+ ions in the solution into Cu0 nanoparticles through bioreduction also ensured the stabilization of the resulting Cu0 nanoparticles. The prepared Camellia Sinensis extract stabilized Cu nanoparticles was characterized using FT-IR, XRD, and TEM spectroscopic methods, and its catalytic activity in the ammonia borane hydrolysis reaction was investigated. The rapid manufactured and quite inexpensive catalyst has been utilized on direct hydrogen production by AB hydrolysis without going through any separation or purification procedures. The effects of catalyst amount, AB concentration, and temperature parameters on Camellia sinensis extract stabilized Cu nanoparticles catalyzed AB hydrolysis kinetics, and the reusability of the catalyst were tested. An environmental friendly catalyst material has been prepared practically in-situ from an easily accessible natural product without requiring any chemical process, and the activation energy, Ea, of the AB hydrolysis reaction has been calculated as 69.96 kJ.mol-1.

10.25781/kaust-htcy9.abstract: Sodalite and sodalite-like frameworks contain cages that can accommodate many guest anions, including trapped electrons in sodalite electrides. However, the encapsulation of hydride ($\mathrmH^-$) has not been reported in sodalites. Hydrides are of interest for hydrogen storage and for catalyzing reactions such as ammonia synthesis. This thesis examines two families: the classical aluminosilicate sodalite, and the rare-earth sodalite-like oxychlorides $\mathrmRE_3O_4Cl$ (RE = Y, Dy), with the common aim of testing whether the sodalite cage can take up hydride anions. In the first part, hydroxy sodalite ($\mathrmNa_8[AlSiO_4]_6(OH)_2 \cdot n\mathrmH_2O$) was used for two routes. First, the cage $\mathrmNaOH$ was removed by Soxhlet extraction to obtain $\mathrmNa_6[AlSiO_4]_6$, a sodalite-electride precursor; the extent of extraction depended strongly on the synthesis route, and a crown ether did not improve it. Second, hydroxy sodalite was reacted with metal hydrides to exchange the cage $\mathrmOH^-$ for $\mathrmH^-$. The reaction with $\mathrmCaH_2$ at 350 °C retained the framework and gave a $\mathrmCa(OH)_2$ by-product, with the change in the first two reflection intensities consistent with $\mathrmOH^-/\mathrmH^-$ exchange. At 600 °C the framework decomposed, while $\mathrmNaH$ gave an amorphous background that prevented the exchange from being followed. In the second part, $\mathrmRE_3(OH)_6(CO_3)Cl$ (RE = Y, Dy) was prepared and calcined to $\mathrmRE_3O_4Cl$. Removing the carbonate required 450 °C rather than the reported 370 °C, though infrared data indicate residual hydroxide, water, and carbonate. Reaction of $\mathrmY_3O_4Cl$ with solid $\mathrmCaH_2$ or $\mathrmNaH$ caused amorphisation, whereas a low-temperature molten hydride flux left the framework intact, though hydride uptake could not be confirmed from laboratory diffraction data. As a $\mathrmCO_2$ hydrogenation support, $\mathrmY_3O_4Cl$ was inactive alone and with copper, but active with cobalt and iron, giving conversions of 33.0% and 5.1% at 350 °C. Both gave mostly methane, while iron also formed longer-chain hydrocarbons through the reverse water–gas shift. Post-reaction analysis showed a severe loss of crystallinity, indicating structural instability under reaction conditions. Overall, both frameworks can host or exchange anions, but their use was limited by the strong confinement of guests in the aluminosilicate cages and by the rare-earth framework's sensitivity to reducing and thermal conditions.
10.25781/kaust-htcy9.title: Ion exchange and structural changes in sodalite and related materials

10.26190/unsworks/32566.abstract: Ammonia, as both a hydrogen carrier and a vital chemical feedstock, represents a promising route for sustainable energy storage and decarbonisation. This thesis focuses on developing advanced catalysts for electrochemical ammonia synthesis via nitrate reduction, combining experimental innovation with computational modelling. The background and foundational principles of the work are introduced based on a comprehensive literature review. The materials, characterisation techniques, and experimental methods used throughout the research are also outlined. Three interconnected projects are presented. First, a liquid metal-based strategy is employed to fabricate bismuth (Bi) nano-electrocatalysts by electrochemically expelling Bi from a Ga–Bi alloy. Through controlled cooling and interfacial perturbations, Bi nanostructures—including nanosheets, nanotubes, and nanoparticles—are formed, with nanoparticles exhibiting the highest current density due to superior surface area and conductivity. These nanostructures are integrated into graphene oxide liquid crystals, creating a hierarchical conductor–catalyst framework. The electrodes, produced via 3D printing, enable precise architecture, enhancing mass transport, electron transfer, and catalyst stability. This system achieves a high ammonia production rate (400 nmol s⁻¹ cm⁻²), over 90% Faradaic efficiency, and current densities exceeding 350 mA cm⁻², surpassing industrial benchmarks. Next, the design of a high-entropy liquid metal alloy (HELMA) catalyst composed of Ga–Fe–Zn–Sn–Bi–Ni is explored. The catalyst is developed using ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) and Design of Experiments (DoE), which reduce the candidate pool to 28 targeted compositions. The liquid state facilitates atomic-level dispersion and dynamic surface reconfiguration. The optimised HELMA achieves a sevenfold improvement in ammonia production (320 nmol s⁻¹ cm⁻²) with 90% Faradaic efficiency over binary systems. This is followed by Density Functional Theory (DFT) calculations to investigate nitrate reduction (NO₃RR) mechanisms on HELMA, considering minimal endothermic energy and reaction energy. Zn initiates nitrate adsorption, Bi and Sn assist in deoxygenation, Ni promotes nitrogen hydrogenation, and Fe serves as a hydrogen reservoir. This hydrogen shuttling mechanism accelerates kinetics and prevents surface poisoning. Finally, the key outcomes are summarised, highlighting the untapped potential of liquid alloys and computational modelling in catalyst development, and outlining directions for future research.

10.26434/chemrxiv.15005664/v1.abstract: The development of electrocatalyst for nearly complete electrocatalytic nitrate reduction without accumulating nitrites in the product feed is indispensable for sustainable nitrate contaminated wastewater treatment and carbon-neutral green ammonia production. In this study, CuFe 2 O 4 nanowires could mimic the bifunctional nature of nitrite reductase where Cu act as nitrate adsorption and deoxygenation center while Fe promoted adsorption of H* and the reduction of *NO to NH 2 . We demonstrate the involvement of a hydride‑transfer pathway supported by obtaining four‑electron transfer from rotating‑disk voltammetry and further corroborated by the mechanistic insights obtained from DFT analysis. The faradaic efficiency for ammonia exceeded 95% at all applied potentials, with an ammonia‑to‑nitrite yield‑rate ratio of 13 at −1.1 V vs. Reversible Hydrogen Electrode. The enhanced nitrite reduction was due to the potential dependent cubic to tetragonal phase transition at higher overpotential exposing undercoordinated iron sites promoting H* adsorption and hydrogenation of *NO. The tandem electrocatalysis mechanism led simultaneously to high NH 3 selectivity, suppressing hydrogen evolution reaction and resulting negligible nitrite accumulation. This work establishes a correlation between ammonia selectivity, surface structure and phase of spinel CuFe 2 O 4 and provides crucial mechanistic insights into reaction pathways of NO 3 - /NO 2 - electroreduction
10.26434/chemrxiv.15005664/v1.title: Potential‑Driven Tetragonal CuFe2O4 Phase Transition Enables Near‑Complete Nitrate‑to‑Ammonia Conversion with Minimal Nitrite Accumulation

10.26434/chemrxiv.15005808/v1.abstract: Driven by the growing need for sustainable ammonia production and effective nitrate remediation, the electrocatalytic nitrate reduction reaction (NO3RR) has emerged as a promising technology. This process enables the conversion of nitrate pollutants into ammonia under mild operating conditions, offering a greener alternative to the energy-intensive Haber–Bosch route. However, the complex multi-electron and multi-proton transfer pathways involved in NO3RR require catalysts capable of precisely regulating intermediate adsorption, activation, and transformation. Atomically precise metal nanoclusters (NCs), with their well-defined atomic structures, tunable electronic properties, and identifiable active sites, have recently attracted considerable attention as model catalysts for elucidating structure–activity relationships. This review discusses the fundamental aspects of NO3RR, including key intermediates and reaction mechanisms, and summarizes recent advances in the use of atomically precise metal NCs for nitrate-to-ammonia conversion. The catalytic performances of mono-, bi-, and trimetallic NCs are systematically compared, highlighting the roles of active-site engineering, ligand modulation, heterometal incorporation, and cluster assembly in regulating activity and selectivity. The review concludes by discussing the key challenges that remain in this field and highlighting future research directions toward the development of NC-based electrocatalysts with enhanced activity, selectivity, and long-term stability for sustainable ammonia production.
10.26434/chemrxiv.15005808/v1.title: Atomically precise metal nanoclusters in nitrate-to-ammonia electrocatalysis

10.26434/chemrxiv.15006312/v1.abstract: Green hydrogen produced from biogas reforming offers a low-carbon feedstock route to sustainable ammonia synthesis, coupling waste valorization with decarbonized fertilizer and chemical production. This review examines the technical foundations of this pathway: the composition and purification of biogas; the principal reforming routes to hydrogen — steam reforming, dry reforming, partial oxidation, and autothermal reforming — together with the catalysts that enable them; the cryogenic air separation required to supply oxygen and nitrogen to the process; and the reactor configurations and catalysts used for ammonia synthesis. The economic evaluation methodology commonly used to assess hydrogen production cost is outlined, alongside a SWOT analysis of green hydrogen production in Egypt, a country with substantial biogas feedstock potential and a strategic export position. Ammonia's principal industrial applications are also summarized. Taken together, this review provides a technical basis for evaluating biogas-derived green hydrogen as a route to sustainable ammonia production, particularly in regions with abundant organic waste streams and growing renewable energy ambitions.

10.26434/chemrxiv.15006347/v1.abstract: Sorption‑enhanced ammonia synthesis (SEAS) requires solid sorbents with high capacity, fast kinetics, and reliable models at elevated temperature and pressure. Here, zeolites and supported metal halides are compared systematically for high‑temperature NH3 sorption for SEAS process design. Commercial zeolites (3A, 4A, 13X, LiLSX) were screened by quasi‑continuous pulse chemisorption (ambient pressure, 50–350 °C), combining capacity determination with TPD‑based site analysis. The most promising candidate LiLSX, still adsorbing NH3 at more than 300 °C, was then benchmarked against supported MnCl2‑based sorbents in a high‑pressure magnetic suspension balance (200–400 °C, up to 12 bar ammonia partial pressure). Morphology and salt distribution were characterized by SEM/EDX. Equilibria were modeled with Langmuir, Toth, Sips and dual‑site Langmuir (DSL) isotherms. NH3 adsorption kinetics on LiLSX were fitted using driving force, stretched exponential (SE) and double SE (DSE) rate expressions. Only LiLSX showed appreciable NH3 uptake above 200 °C in pulse chemisorption and remains active at 300 °C and 0.1 bar ammonia partial pressure. TPD signal and isotherm modeling confirm adsorption on two site types. At SEAS‑relevant conditions, LiLSX attained on average ~40 % higher NH3 capacity than MnCl2(30 wt.%)/AC. LiLSX sustained a quasi‑stable working capacity over 90 adsorption–desorption cycles at 300–350 °C without detectable structural damage. Among all kinetic models tested, the DSE approach best captures LiLSX NH3 uptake behavior and reflects two characteristic time scales aligned with the dual‑site equilibrium description. The presented methodology and model parameters directly support the design and simulation of SEAS reactors.
10.26434/chemrxiv.15006347/v1.title: High temperature and pressure sorption of ammonia using zeolites and supported metal halides: experimental investigations and sorption modeling

10.26434/chemrxiv.15006354/v1.abstract: This paper presents the process design, steady-state simulation, and mechanical sizing of a cryogenic air separation unit (ASU) developed as part of a sustainable ammonia production flowsheet from biogas. The unit uses Linde double-column cryogenic distillation to separate atmospheric air (modeled as a ternary O2/N2/Ar mixture) into a high-purity nitrogen stream for ammonia synthesis and an oxygen stream for autothermal reforming of biogas-derived methane. The process was simulated in Aspen HYSYS at a feed rate of 1300 kmol/h, achieving a nitrogen product purity of 99.883% and an oxygen product purity of 95.04%. Detailed plate hydraulic design (Souders-Brown flooding, weeping, entrainment, and downcomer back-up checks) and AIChE tray-efficiency calculations were carried out for both the high-pressure column (HPC) and low-pressure column (LPC), followed by mechanical design of the pressure vessels and an equipment cost estimate. The low-pressure column required 30 theoretical trays (41 actual stages) at a diameter of 1.746 m, with an estimated 2024-indexed cost of $380,368. A reflux-ratio/number-of-stages optimization was performed for the high-pressure column to identify the trade-off between operating and fixed costs. The results demonstrate a technically sound and economically quantified ASU design suitable for integration into a green ammonia production route.
10.26434/chemrxiv.15006354/v1.title: Design and Simulation of a Cryogenic Air Separation Unit for a Biogas-to-Ammonia Process

10.26434/chemrxiv.15006589/v1.abstract: Renewable-electricity-powered hydrogen supply chains require compact, efficient, and demand-responsive NH3 crackers. Here we develop a microwave-driven ammonia decomposition system based on an LTA-type zeolite catalyst loaded with 10 wt% Ru nanoparticles that directly converts electrical energy into chemical energy through localized catalyst heating. The system achieves an external energy conversion efficiency of 48%, based on the net microwave input power after subtracting the reflected power. Thermal simulations further reveal an internal energy conversion efficiency of 60%, based on the microwave energy absorbed by the catalyst, independent of microwave frequency, corresponding to a hydrogen production efficiency of 92% on a lower heating value (LHV) basis. The reactor maintains high reaction rates while keeping the reactor wall at only 450 °C, enabling the use of conventional stainless steels. Multiphysics simulations combined with in situ synchrotron total scattering reveal that the dielectric properties of the zeolite support promote efficient power-to-chemical energy conversion by localizing electromagnetic energy within the catalyst. Fast start-up, rapid shutdown, and stable operation under fluctuating power demonstrate a compact and demand-responsive platform for decentralized hydrogen production compatible with renewable electricity.

10.26434/chemrxiv.15006680/v1.abstract: The development of catalytic systems capable of ammonia synthesis under milder conditions remains an important challenge. Recent experimental studies have reported enhanced ammonia formation over gallium–copper liquid metal catalysts. Here, we integrate machine-learning interatomic potentials, well-tempered metadynamics, and electronic-structure analysis to elucidate the reaction mechanism and the role of copper in catalysis. Transiently exposed Cu atoms selectively promote H2 dissociation through favorable Cu–H orbital interactions, whereas they provide negligible π back-donation to N2 and therefore do not significantly facilitate N–N bond activation. Consequently, the computed free-energy landscape favors an associative pathway in which sequential hydrogenation precedes N–N bond cleavage. While Cu does not uniformly lower the barriers for all elementary steps, it selectively stabilizes early hydrogenated intermediates, thereby making the overall reaction thermodynamically more favorable.
10.26434/chemrxiv.15006680/v1.title: Mechanistic Insights into Ammonia Formation on Dynamic Liquid Metal Catalysts

10.26599/nr.2026.94908519.abstract: Abstract It is non-trivial to perform density functional theory (DFT) screening for experimental validation that can accelerate qualitative materials discovery to give priority to the top candidates. Cluster catalysts, owing to their adequate active sites, quantum effect, high ratio of volume/surface, excellent activity and selectivity, have garnered widespread attention in various complicated multi-step catalytic reactions. However, the design concept, structure formation principle, electrocatalysis process and potential reaction mechanism are rarely unveiled. This perspective will summarize the DFT calculation-assisted screening concept with emphasis on theoretical calculation descriptor, geometric structures, electronic properties, adsorption behaviors, and reaction mechanism to monitor the cluster catalysis. Thereafter, experimental design of advanced clusters will be presented, including synthetic strategies and various characterization techniques for intrinsic active sites identification. Subsequently, an overview of the structure-property correlation to drive diverse electrochemical reactions will be exemplified and discussed, encompassing cathode reaction of oxygen reduction reaction (ORR), anode oxidation of H2, alcohols and acids, water splitting, nitrogen reduction reaction (NRR), carbon dioxide reduction reaction (CO2RR). Finally, a fundamental insight into the existing challenges and perspectives were proposed for rational screening and structural regulation of the advanced clusters for the electrochemical reactions in clean energy conversion devices.
